Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, a very warm welcome to this UN action side event. Thank you all for being here. Not much else going on this week, aside from 166 other side events. We greatly appreciate your participation. My name is Letitia Anderson. I'm the coordinator of UN Action Against Sexual Violence in Conflict, and I'm very pleased to moderate today's event, Inaction is Not an Option, From Knowledge to Prevention, the UN Action Approach to Addressing CRSV. I extend our deepest gratitude to the European Union as lead supporter of UN Action's knowledge building work and to our 13 other esteemed co-sponsors, Austria, Belgium, Canada, Finland, France, Ireland, Japan, Lithuania, Norway, Portugal, Spain, Sweden and the United Kingdom. Your steadfast political resolve and resources has made our collective action possible. And collective action is indeed critical, as this is a crime that lays bare the horrors and human costs of war. We are all here to deepen our knowledge and better understand the history of this scourge in order to deny it a future. To set the scene, it is my honor to give the floor to the Special Representative of the Secretary General on Sexual Violence in Conflict and Chair of the UN Action Network, Under-Secretary-General Pramila Patten, to deliver opening remarks and formally launch the new UN Action Toolkit on a survivor-centered approach. And I must say, this is extremely fitting. as SRSG Patten has worked tirelessly to prioritize prevention and center survivors since the start of her tenure in 2017. SRSG, you have the floor.

Thank you, Excellencies, distinguished participants and colleagues. Throughout the history of warfare, sexual violence, more than any other atrocity, has been routinely dismissed as inevitable. The result has been centuries of silencing and sidelining the experiences of survivors. By treating this violence as inevitable, inaction and indifference also became inevitable. In 2007, when UN Action launched its signature Stop Rape Now campaign, it called for a paradigm shift. It debunked the myth of inevitability, which shielded perpetrators, normalized sexual violence, and reduced survivors to the unavoidable collateral damage of war. Instead, it called for conflict-related sexual violence to be elevated onto the international peace and security agenda as a threat that is preventable, not inevitable, and for which inaction is not an option. The evidence bears this out. Patterns of sexual violence vary dramatically between conflicts and armed groups across time and space. And this variation tells us that violence or restraint is shaped by policy choices, incentives, command structures, normative frameworks, and consequences for noncompliance. Even the most extreme belligerent behavior is subject to change. Today, nearly two decades after the establishment of UN action, The question is no longer whether conflict-related sexual violence can be prevented, but how we can prevent it most effectively. One of the clearest lessons learned in this agenda is that applying a survivor-centered approach is not just a matter of ethics, it is a matter of effectiveness. Survivors are not just repositories of past stories. They are custodians of knowledge that can shape a safer future. Across many war-torn corners of the world, I have met survivors who are working in their communities as agents of change and architects of peace. It is vital to ensure that their voices and choices shape the global search for solutions. To that end, Security Council Resolution 2467 of 2019 called for a survivor-centered approach to inform all prevention and response efforts. The new UN Action Toolkit we are launching today will help to translate this promise into practice through a model that shifts power back to the survivor. The toolkit developed with survivors for practitioners provides practical guidance to ensure that interventions center the rights, needs and wishes of survivors, recognizing that they are not a homogeneous group, but face intersecting forms of discrimination. This addition to UN Action's Global Knowledge Hub builds on other pioneering tools, such as the matrix of early warning indicators developed to translate early warning signs into early action, and also the prevention framework, which articulates a two-track approach, namely primary prevention to address the root causes, drivers, and enabling conditions before conflict-related sexual violence occurs, and secondary prevention to mitigate the risk of stigma and reprisals that follow in its wake. Indeed, the true measure of success is the atrocity that never occurs, the life that is not irreversibly divided into before and after an unimaginable tragedy. As survivors everywhere have consistently told me, what happened to me could have been prevented. or no other woman or girl should have to suffer as I did. Today, we know more than ever before about the risk and repercussions of conflict-related sexual violence. And this makes our collective responsibility even greater. And it is time to move from best intentions to best practice. Yet, these crimes, which should have been relegated to the history books, continue to be repeated in our daily headlines. Last year, my mandate reported almost 10,000 UN-verified cases of sexual violence used as a tactic of war, torture, terror, and political repression. The trend lines are worsening, reflecting the widening scope of warfare globally, runaway military spending, arms proliferation, and record levels of forced displacement. Everything we know and are able to report about these crimes stems from the courage of survivors who risk stigma, reprisals, rejection, and public humiliation to come forward. They cannot be expected to do so in the absence of assistance. It is time to defend human dignity, not defund essential services. The founding vision of UN Action was to bridge sectoral silos to deliver a holistic response that meets survivors' needs, from medical care to psychological support, socioeconomic reintegration, and access to justice. Rather than being forced to navigate fragmented systems, we bring the system together around the survivor. UN Action has established and equipped integrated service centers in the DRC, Mali, Sudan, Ukraine, and elsewhere. In South Sudan, support for survivors linked recovery with economic empowerment. In Somalia, reintegration programs help women formerly associated with Al-Shabaab to rebuild their lives and livelihoods. These projects have harnessed digital technology for safe and confidential referrals, as well as using mobile clinics to reach survivors in remote, volatile regions. The lessons learned are continually collated into our knowledge hub to inform the next generation of practice. Excellencies, at this critical moment of gender equality backlash, rising reprisals, cascading crisis, and contracting aid budgets, We must stand together on the right side of history as partners of progress. As the threat environment evolves, UN action continues to hold a mirror up to the changing face of war, deepening knowledge on technology-facilitated violence and intersections with food insecurity and climate shocks. It continues to ensure that the UN system is equipped with information and resources to operate collectively and effectively. When I reflect on what is at stake, I think of the grandmother I met in South Sudan caring for a seven-year-old granddaughter who had been raped in the very displacement camp to which they had fled for safety. I think of the young woman in eastern DRC who was gang-raped by militia in retaliation for speaking out against sexual violence and driven from her home. I think of the Rohingya woman who said, "The sexual violence I endured broke my heart and my mind, but not my spirit." Unfortunately, such voices are still too rarely heard in these halls. As world leaders gather to confront the global challenges of our time, we cannot allow the plight and rights of survivors to be forgotten. To the many governments and esteemed partners present in this room, my call to action is twofold. First, ensure a survivor-centered, trauma-informed approach by integrating the UN Action Toolkit into all plans, policies and programs as the new global standard. Second, sustain investment for its implementation by providing urgently needed funding to the UN Action Network through its Multi-Partner Trust Fund to close critical protection and assistance gaps. Excellencies, in line with the theme of this year's General Assembly, that is how we will rebuild trust with conflict-affected communities and ultimately deliver for all. 81 years ago, this organization was founded to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war. Today, that promise must include the persistent yet preventable scourge of wartime rape. Thank you.

The UK survivor advisory group brings together survivors from across the world to shape our action, using their lived experience to help identify what works and challenge assumptions. Fourth, as the risks evolve, our response must evolve with them. Not only because it reduces harm, but because it helps create the conditions for lasting peace, equality and security. We have the evidence, we have the experience, we have the commitments.
